description:
The idea: Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map 🔴
Mars has no GPS. If an astronaut loses comms or electronics, how do they find their way back to safety?

We’ll build a Martian survival map showing water ice, shelter, hazards and safe routes, plus an offline “you are here” locator that finds your position from the stars, the Sun, and Mars’ moons, Phobos and Deimos. The map shows where to go, and the stars tell you where you are.
summary: Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map is a navigation tool for astronauts who lose communications or electronics on Mars, where there is no GPS and no compass. It has two parts. The first is a survival map built in QGIS from NASA and USGS data. It uses MOLA elevation, contours, hillshade, official place names, surface roughness and thermal inertia, and high-resolution CTX images of Jezero crater and the InSight landing site. Together these show steep slopes, rough or soft ground, hazards and safe routes, as a base for marking water ice and shelter. The second is an offline "you are here" locator that works like sailors' star navigation. You measure the time Phobos or Deimos is highest in the sky and how high it is. Our Python program uses NASA JPL Horizons data to turn these into latitude and longitude, then shows the position on a map. Using both moons improves accuracy. We designed a small sky camera to make the measurement automatic, with the Sun and stars as backups. The map shows where to go, and the sky shows where you are: a simple, low-cost backup navigation method that does not depend on satellites.
details:
Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map

Mars has no GPS, no navigation satellites and no global magnetic field, so a compass does not work. If an astronaut loses communications or electronics, how do they find their way back to safety? Our project answers two questions: "Where should I go?" and "Where am I?"

1) The survival map (where to go)

We built a multi-layer map of Mars in QGIS using NASA and USGS planetary data. The base layer is the MOLA digital elevation model (463 m/pixel) in pseudocolour, with 5,000 m contour lines and a hillshade layer blended on top, so steep slopes and cliffs are easy to see. We added the official IAU feature names (craters, mountains, canyons), surface data such as TES thermal inertia and MOLA roughness (dust, sand or solid rock, smooth or rough ground), and detailed CTX image mosaics of Jezero crater (6 m/pixel) and the InSight landing area. Along the Perseverance route we mapped geological units such as regolith, ripples, crater ejecta blocks and crater rims, which show what ground is safe and what is a hazard. The goal is a survival guide that shows water ice, shelter, hazards and safe routes.

2) The "you are here" locator (where you are)

Phobos and Deimos orbit almost exactly above the Martian equator. An observer measures two things for each moon: the exact UTC time it is highest in the sky, and its height above the horizon. The time gives longitude: our Python program asks NASA JPL Horizons which point on Mars was directly under the moon at that moment. The height gives latitude: the lower the moon looks, the further you are from the equator. The direction the moon moves (Phobos rises in the west, Deimos in the east) tells whether you are north or south of it, without a compass. Both moons give one position each, and the average improves accuracy. The program draws your position on a map of Mars. Our concept for a fully automatic version is a small all-sky camera with a level sensor and a clock that detects the moons itself. The Sun and stars can be used the same way when the moons are not visible.

Benefits and impact: a simple and low-cost backup navigation method for astronauts and rovers, which works without satellites. It combines "where to go" (the map) and "where am I" (the sky) in one survival tool.

Tools: QGIS, Python (built-in libraries only), NASA JPL Horizons API, HTML/SVG for the map output.

Creativity: we use the two Martian moons the way sailors used the stars, and we combine real NASA mission data into a practical survival guide.

Factors considered: accuracy (about 1 degree of height error gives roughly 35–50 km of position error), when each moon can be seen (Phobos up to about 69° latitude, Deimos up to about 82°), the small tilt of the moons' orbits (corrected using NASA data), and keeping the hardware small, light and low-power.
